title: Deep Q-Learning on Hölder Spaces

paper.title: Deep Q-Learning on Hölder Spaces
paper.abstract: Abstract We study the operator-theoretic core of Q-learning in continuous-time stochastic control with continuous states and actions. In value-based reinforcement learning, each Q-learning or DQN update is built from a Bellman optimality target; our analysis isolates this target in a diffusion setting and studies its regularity and approximation complexity. Under uniform ellipticity and Hölder-regular coefficients, we show that a Bellman update maps bounded inputs into an anisotropic regularity class, smoothing the state variable while leaving only Lipschitz dependence on the action variable. This yields a compact family of Bellman iterates and motivates a tensor-product DeepONet architecture adapted to the mixed regularity of the problem. We then derive explicit approximation and resource bounds, together with a stiffness–complexity trade-off as the time step δ → 0 \delta\to 0 . The resulting theory makes a direct contribution to Q-learning theory at the level of Bellman target regularity and approximation in continuous stochastic control. At the same time, we do not claim a full convergence theorem for practical sampled Q-learning with exploration, replay, and stochastic gradient updates.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: This paper studies the operator-theoretic core of Q-learning in continuous-time stochastic control with continuous states and actions. In value-based reinforcement learning, the central object is the Bellman optimality update for the action-value function; every Q-learning or DQN step is, at heart, an attempt to approximate this update from data. Our focus is on this Bellman target itself in a continuous-time diffusion model, where the coefficients are known and the operator can be analyzed directly. This does not yet cover all ingredients of practical Q-learning, but it does address what we view as one of its core theoretical questions: what regularity and approximation complexity does the Bellman target class possess? The relationship with Q-learning can be stated concretely. In discrete time, a typical value-based target has the form r + β ​ max a ′ ⁡ Q ⁡ ( x ′ , a ′ ) r+\beta\max_{a^{\prime}}Q(x^{\prime},a^{\prime}) , namely a stochastic approximation to a Bellman optimality operator. Our continuous-time discretization replaces the single sampled transition by its conditional expectation over a short diffusion step of size δ \delta , thereby isolating the operator-level part of the theory from the separate issues of exploration, replay, and stochastic optimization. This is why we view the paper as a contribution to Q-learning theory, while also being explicit that it operates at the Bellman-operator level. Classical analyses of value-based methods with function approximation often assume that the transition and reward coefficients are globally Lipschitz in state and action. While convenient, this hypothesis misses a central feature of stochastic control: non-degenerate diffusion can regularize the Bellman update through parabolic smoothing. In PDE language, the Bellman step is tied to a controlled parabolic equation, so rough inputs may become more regular after one application of the operator ( Krylov, 1987 ) . Motivated by this observation, we study the time-discretized Bellman optimality operator 𝒯 δ \mathcal{T}_{\delta} under uniform ellipticity and Hölder-regular coefficients. The main message is that the Bellman targets underlying value-based learning in this regime lie in an anisotropic regularity class substantially smaller than a generic Lipschitz class. This creates an approximation-theoretic route toward neural architectures tailored to the regularity of continuous-control Bellman iterates, and hence toward a sharper theory of what Q-learning-style methods are trying to approximate in this setting.

sections.heading: 1.1 Main Contributions
sections.text: Our contributions are fourfold. First, we prove that under uniform ellipticity the Bellman operator maps bounded inputs into an anisotropic Hölder class: smooth in the state variable and only Lipschitz in the action variable. This identifies a nontrivial regularity structure for the Bellman targets that arise in continuous-time Q-learning problems. Second, we show that this regularity statement is already a core theoretical contribution to Q-learning: it describes the target class that any value-function approximator must represent in this diffusion regime. The operator-theoretic viewpoint is therefore not peripheral to Q-learning, but rather isolates its mathematical backbone. Third, we use this regularity to derive approximation guarantees for a tensor-product DeepONet architecture that approximates Bellman iterates. The architecture is chosen because it matches the anisotropic regularity revealed by the Bellman analysis; the regularity statement itself is architecture-independent, while the theorem provides one constructive approximation route. Fourth, we quantify the stiffness–complexity trade-off induced by the time step δ \delta . As δ → 0 \delta\to 0 , the Bellman operator approaches the identity and the smoothing effect weakens, which increases the approximation complexity. This explains why continuous-time limits can become numerically stiff even when the diffusion is regularizing. Overall, the paper aims to make a precise claim: in continuous stochastic control with uniformly elliptic diffusion, the Bellman targets at the heart of Q-learning enjoy exploitable anisotropic regularity, and this has concrete consequences for approximation theory and architecture design. What we do not claim is a full convergence theorem for sampled Q-learning with exploration, replay, target-network heuristics, and stochastic gradient optimization.

sections.heading: 1.2 Literature Review
sections.text: Our work sits at the intersection of approximation theory for Deep Learning, stochastic analysis of PDEs, and reinforcement learning. We briefly survey the relevant literature in these domains. The convergence of Q-learning with function approximation has been a central topic since the early work of Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1996) . The empirical success of DQN was popularized by Mnih et al. (2015) , while rigorous analyses of value-based methods with function approximation often impose strong smoothness or contraction assumptions; see, for example, Fan et al. (2020) . Our work addresses a complementary but, in our view, foundational theoretical question: what regularity and approximation complexity do the Bellman targets themselves possess in a continuous-time stochastic-control regime? Because Q-learning and DQN are built around repeated approximation of Bellman optimality targets, understanding this target class is already a direct contribution to Q-learning theory, even before one adds finite-sample and optimization analysis. The observations of Tallec et al. (2019) about stiffness as δ → 0 \delta\to 0 , of Qi (2025) about regularity collapse near decision boundaries, and of Qi (2026) about viscosity-consistency constraints for deep Q-network discretizations help motivate our complexity discussion. At the same time, to avoid overstatement, we emphasize that our theorem is an operator-level approximation result for Bellman iterates in a diffusion setting, not a full convergence guarantee for practical sampled Q-learning training dynamics. The correspondence between the Bellman equation and parabolic PDEs is classical, established by Krylov (1980) and Fleming and Soner (2006) . While the existence of viscosity solutions for HJB equations is well-known ( Crandall et al., 1992 ) , the application of interior regularity estimates to analyze the sample complexity of RL is relatively new. Most existing finite-sample bounds for RL ( Azar et al., 2017 ; Jin et al., 2018 ) operate in the tabular or linear setting. In contrast, our work explicitly utilizes the anisotropic nature of the Schauder estimates ( C 2 , α C^{2,\alpha} in state, C 0 , 1 C^{0,1} in action) induced by the diffusion term Tr ​ ( σ ​ σ ⊤ ​ D 2 ​ V ) \text{Tr}(\sigma\sigma^{\top}D^{2}V) , a concept deeply rooted in the theory of regularization by noise. Universal Approximation Theorems (UATs) for neural networks have evolved from qualitative density results ( Cybenko, 1989 ; Hornik, 1991 ) to quantitative complexity bounds. Yarotsky (2017) established the relationship between network depth/width and the Sobolev regularity of the target function, showing that W ∼ ϵ − d / s W\sim\epsilon^{-d/s} . However, applying these isotropic bounds to Q ∗ Q^{*} yields pessimistic estimates due to the joint dimension d state + d action d_{\text{state}}+d_{\text{action}} . Our analysis circumvents this by adopting the anisotropic viewpoint of Mhaskar and Poggio (2016) and Poggio et al. (2017) , decoupling the complexity of the smooth state manifold from the non-smooth policy landscape. The architecture proposed in this paper draws upon the emerging field of Operator Learning. The Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), introduced by Lu et al. (2021) , generalizes the universal approximation theorem to non-linear operators on Banach spaces. Similarly, the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) ( Li et al., 2021 ) has shown success in solving PDEs by learning the solution operator directly. While these methods are primarily applied to forward problems in fluid dynamics and solid mechanics, we adapt the framework to the backward Bellman flow. Our Tensor-Product Trunk modification addresses the specific mixed-regularity requirements of the Control problem, which are not typically present in physical conservation laws.

Unlike standard RL theory which relies on the contraction property to preserve Lipschitz continuity, we utilize the regularizing effect of the diffusion term σ ​ σ ⊤ \sigma\sigma^{\top} . sections.heading: 3.4 Implication for Neural Approximation
sections.text: The compactness result (Corollary 15 ) provides the rigorous foundation for approximating Q ∗ Q^{*} using deep neural networks. Standard universal approximation theorems often assume the target function lies in a generic Sobolev space W k , p W^{k,p} , leading to pessimistic bounds on the required network size due to the Curse of Dimensionality. Our PDE analysis offers a more precise characterization via the concept of Metric Entropy .

sections.heading: Metric Entropy and Covering Numbers
sections.text: Let 𝒬 δ ∗ ⊂ ℋ α , Lip \mathcal{Q}^{*}_{\delta}\subset\mathcal{H}^{\alpha,\text{Lip}} be the set of reachable Q-functions for a fixed time-step δ \delta . The complexity of learning this class is governed by its Kolmogorov ϵ \epsilon -entropy, log ⁡ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ϵ , 𝒬 δ ∗ ) \log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{Q}^{*}_{\delta}) , where 𝒩 \mathcal{N} is the covering number (the minimal number of balls of radius ϵ \epsilon required to cover the set). For the Hölder ball of radius R R in dimension d d with smoothness s s , the entropy scales as: log ⁡ 𝒩 ⁡ ( ϵ , Ball R ​ ( C s ) ) ≍ ( R ϵ ) d / s . \log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\text{Ball}_{R}(C^{s}))\asymp\left(\frac{R}{\epsilon}\right)^{d/s}. (27) In our context, the effective smoothness in the state space is s = 2 + α s=2+\alpha . This implies that the diffusion term effectively reduces the complexity of the function class compared to the standard Lipschitz assumption ( s = 1 s=1 ), where the exponent would be d d .

sections.heading: The Complexity-Stability Trade-off
sections.text: However, we must address the dependency on the time discretization δ \delta . From the smoothing estimate ( 20 ), the radius of the function class scales as R ≈ O ⁡ ( δ − 1 + α 2 ) R\approx O(\delta^{-\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}) . Consequently, the network complexity required to achieve an error ϵ \epsilon scales roughly as: Complexity ​ ( δ , ϵ ) ∼ ( 1 δ 1 + α 2 ​ ϵ ) d 2 + α . \text{Complexity}(\delta,\epsilon)\sim\left(\frac{1}{\delta^{\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{d}{2+\alpha}}. (28) This reveals a fundamental trade-off: • Smoothing Benefit: For a fixed δ \delta , the parabolic nature of the Bellman operator constrains the target functions to a smooth manifold, making them efficiently learnable. • Stiffness Cost: As δ → 0 \delta\to 0 (approximating the continuous-time control limit), the Bellman operator approaches the Identity, and the smoothing effect acts over an infinitesimally small time. The functions become stiff (large second derivatives), inflating the constant R R and requiring larger networks (increased width/depth) to resolve the sharp curvatures near decision boundaries.

sections.heading: Anisotropic Inductive Bias
sections.text: The distinction between state and action regularity dictates a specific inductive bias for the network architecture. A standard Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) treating ( x , a ) (x,a) as a concatenated vector represents an isotropic prior. Corollary 15 suggests that the optimal architecture should be anisotropic : • The state subnet should utilize smooth activation functions (e.g., tanh \tanh , SiLU) to match the C x 2 , α C^{2,\alpha}_{x} regularity. • The action subnet should utilize piecewise-linear activations (e.g., ReLU) to model the potentially non-smooth ( C a 0 , 1 C^{0,1}_{a} ) dependence and the sharp transitions induced by the max \max operator. This motivates the specific design of the Operator-Network proposed in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4 Universal Approximation Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we establish the convergence rate of the proposed Neural Operator scheme. A rigorous analysis must address the anisotropic nature of the value function regularity established in Section 3 : the Bellman iterates exhibit parabolic smoothing in the state space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} but remain merely Lipschitz continuous in the action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . Standard isotropic approximations (e.g., standard MLPs) suffer from the curse of dimensionality over the combined dimension d + d a d+d_{a} . We prove that our Tensor-Product DeepONet architecture (Section A.2 ) successfully decouples these complexities, allowing the parabolic smoothing to reduce the effective dimension of the state space without being bottlenecked by the action space geometry.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We have established an approximation-theoretic framework for Bellman value iteration in continuous stochastic control by grounding the analysis in the uniform ellipticity of the environment noise rather than restrictive global Lipschitz assumptions. By exploiting interior Schauder estimates, we proved that the Bellman operator maps bounded iterates into the anisotropic Hölder space C x 2 , α ​ ( 𝒮 ) × C a 0 , 1 ​ ( 𝒜 ) C^{2,\alpha}_{x}(\mathcal{S})\times C^{0,1}_{a}(\mathcal{A}) . Our proposed Tensor-Product DeepONet architecture explicitly leverages this mixed regularity, decoupling the smooth state manifold from the non-smooth policy landscape to mitigate the curse of dimensionality. Crucially, we quantified the stiffness–complexity trade-off, proving that the required network capacity scales as 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ − γ ⁡ ( α ) ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(\delta^{-\gamma(\alpha)d}) due to the singularity of the heat kernel as δ → 0 \delta\to 0 . We further validated the restriction to compact domains via the exponential decay of diffusion exit probabilities. We view these results as a core theoretical contribution to Q-learning in the continuous-time diffusion regime: they characterize the regularity and approximation complexity of the Bellman targets that value-based methods are built to learn. What the paper does not provide is a full convergence theorem for practical Deep Q-Learning with exploration, replay, and stochastic optimization. Rather, it isolates the Bellman side of the theory and shows that, in this regime, those targets enjoy exploitable anisotropic regularity and admit quantifiable approximation guarantees. acknowledgments-disclosure-of-funding. sections.heading: Appendix A Operator-Based Network Architecture
sections.text: To leverage the smoothing properties established in Section 3 , we propose a network architecture designed to approximate the operator map 𝒯 δ : C ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) → C x 2 , α ​ ( 𝒟 ) \mathcal{T}_{\delta}:C(\mathcal{D})\to C^{2,\alpha}_{x}(\mathcal{D}) . Consequently, we adopt a mesh-free approach based on the Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) framework ( Lu et al., 2021 ) , which generalizes the universal approximation theorem to non-linear operators on Banach spaces.

sections.heading: A.1 The DeepONet Framework
sections.text: We seek a neural operator 𝒩 θ \mathcal{N}_{\theta} that approximates the Bellman transition map 𝒯 δ : ℋ α , Lip → ℋ α , Lip \mathcal{T}_{\delta}:\mathcal{H}^{\alpha,\text{Lip}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\alpha,\text{Lip}} . Following the Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) framework ( Lu et al., 2021 ) , we decompose the architecture into a Branch Net (which encodes the input function space) and a Trunk Net (which encodes the output domain).

sections.heading: A.1.1 Sensor Discretization and Encoding
sections.text: A fundamental challenge in operator learning is that the input to the network is a function, an infinite-dimensional object. In practice, we access the function via a finite set of observations. Let { z j } j = 1 m ⊂ 𝒮 × 𝒜 \{z_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}\subset\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A} be a fixed set of m m sensor locations . We define the discretization operator 𝒫 m : C ⁡ ( 𝒮 × 𝒜 ) → ℝ m \mathcal{P}_{m}:C(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})\to\mathbb{R}^{m} as: 𝒫 m ​ ( Q ) ≔ [ Q ⁡ ( z 1 ) , Q ⁡ ( z 2 ) , … , Q ⁡ ( z m ) ] ⊤ . \mathcal{P}_{m}(Q)\coloneqq\left[Q(z_{1}),Q(z_{2}),\dots,Q(z_{m})\right]^{\top}. (31) In the context of RL, these sensors correspond to the states stored in a Replay Buffer or a fixed quadrature grid used for fitting the value iteration.

sections.heading: A.1.2 Network Definition
sections.text: The Deep Bellman Operator Network is defined as the map 𝒩 θ : ℝ m × ( 𝒮 × 𝒜 ) → ℝ \mathcal{N}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A})\to\mathbb{R} . Let Q i ​ n Q_{in} be the value function from the previous iteration. The approximate next iterate Q ^ o ​ u ​ t ​ ( x , a ) \hat{Q}_{out}(x,a) is given by the inner product of the Branch and Trunk outputs: Q ^ o ​ u ​ t ( x , a ) ≈ 𝒩 θ ( 𝒫 m ( Q i ​ n ) ) ( x , a ) = ∑ k = 1 p b k ​ ( Q i ​ n ​ ( z 1 ) , … , Q i ​ n ​ ( z m ) ) ⏟ Branch Net ​ β : ℝ m → ℝ p ⋅ τ k ​ ( x , a ) ⏟ Trunk Net ​ τ : 𝒮 × 𝒜 → ℝ p + b 0 . \hat{Q}_{out}(x,a)\approx\mathcal{N}_{\theta}(\mathcal{P}_{m}(Q_{in}))(x,a)=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\underbrace{b_{k}\left(Q_{in}(z_{1}),\dots,Q_{in}(z_{m})\right)}_{\text{Branch Net }\beta:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}}\cdot\underbrace{\tau_{k}(x,a)}_{\text{Trunk Net }\tau:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}}+b_{0}. (32) Here, θ \theta represents the trainable weights of the neural networks β \beta and τ \tau . • The Branch Net β \beta learns to extract a latent embedding (coefficients) of the current value landscape from the sensor readings. • The Trunk Net τ \tau learns a continuous basis for the image space of the Bellman operator. Remark 17 (The Role of Sensor Density) . The standard Universal Approximation Theorem for Operators assumes the input is the entire function Q i ​ n Q_{in} . By using 𝒫 m ​ ( Q i ​ n ) \mathcal{P}_{m}(Q_{in}) , we introduce an encoding error (or aliasing error). However, Corollary 15 guarantees that Q i ​ n Q_{in} belongs to a compact subset of the Hölder space ℋ α , Lip \mathcal{H}^{\alpha,\text{Lip}} . Let h = sup y ∈ 𝒮 × 𝒜 min j ⁡ ‖ y − z j ‖ h=\sup_{y\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\min_{j}\|y-z_{j}\| be the fill-distance of the sensors. Due to the Hölder continuity of the inputs, the reconstruction error is bounded by L ​ h α Lh^{\alpha} . Thus, as the number of sensors m → ∞ m\to\infty (and h → 0 h\to 0 ), the discrete representation 𝒫 m ​ ( Q i ​ n ) \mathcal{P}_{m}(Q_{in}) uniquely characterizes Q i ​ n Q_{in} up to arbitrary precision, making the operator approximation well-posed.

sections.heading: A.2 Anisotropic Trunk Architecture
sections.text: The structural results of Corollary 15 indicate that the target functions exhibit mixed regularity: they are locally C 2 , α C^{2,\alpha} in the state variable x x (due to parabolic smoothing) but only Lipschitz continuous in the action variable a a (due to the parametric nature of the operator and the supremum envelope). A standard isotropic MLP (e.g., fully connected layers on concatenated inputs [ x , a ] [x,a] ) fails to exploit this structure efficiently. Furthermore, a full tensor-product basis (via the Kronecker product of feature vectors) would result in a feature dimension scaling quadratically with the width. To remedy this, we propose a Separable Rank- p p Trunk Architecture that explicitly forces a low-rank decomposition of the state-action coupling. Definition 18 (Separable Rank- p p Trunk) . The Trunk Network τ ⁡ ( x , a ) : 𝒮 × 𝒜 → ℝ p \tau(x,a):\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} is constructed as the Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication) of two independent sub-networks. This enforces that the learned basis functions are separable: τ ⁡ ( x , a ) = 𝒩 state ​ ( x , θ x ) ⊙ 𝒩 action ​ ( a , θ a ) . \tau(x,a)=\mathcal{N}_{\text{state}}(x;\theta_{x})\odot\mathcal{N}_{\text{action}}(a;\theta_{a}). (33) Here, ⊙ \odot denotes the element-wise product. Consequently, the k k -th component of the trunk output is given by τ k ​ ( x , a ) = ϕ k ​ ( x ) ​ ψ k ​ ( a ) \tau_{k}(x,a)=\phi_{k}(x)\psi_{k}(a) , where: (i) The State Basis ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) = 𝒩 state ​ ( ⋅ ) : ℝ d → ℝ p \phi(\cdot)=\mathcal{N}_{\text{state}}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} employs smooth activation functions σ s ∈ C ∞ ​ ( ℝ ) \sigma_{s}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) (e.g., tanh \tanh , SiLU) to match the C 2 , α ​ ( 𝒮 ) C^{2,\alpha}(\mathcal{S}) regularity of the heat kernel eigenfunctions. (ii) The Action Basis ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) = 𝒩 action ​ ( ⋅ ) : ℝ d a → ℝ p \psi(\cdot)=\mathcal{N}_{\text{action}}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} employs piecewise-linear activation functions σ r \sigma_{r} (e.g., ReLU) to capture the non-differentiable transitions of the optimal policy.

sections.heading: Theoretical Justification
sections.text: The Hadamard formulation in ( 33 ) combined with the DeepONet inner product ( 32 ) implies that the network approximates the target function Q ^ \hat{Q} via a Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition of rank p p : Q ^ ​ ( x , a ) = ∑ k = 1 p β k ​ ( Q i ​ n ) ⋅ ϕ k ​ ( x ) ⋅ ψ k ​ ( a ) . \hat{Q}(x,a)=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\beta_{k}(Q_{in})\cdot\phi_{k}(x)\cdot\psi_{k}(a). (34) This is structurally distinct from a full Tensor Product basis (which would imply terms of the form ϕ i ​ ( x ) ​ ψ j ​ ( a ) \phi_{i}(x)\psi_{j}(a) for all pairs). While a full tensor product avoids any structural constraints on the state-action coupling, it suffers from an interaction parameter complexity of 𝒪 ⁡ ( p 2 ) \mathcal{O}(p^{2}) . To justify the restriction to a diagonal (rank- p p ) structure, we must carefully distinguish between the spatial smoothing of the PDE and the parametric dependence on the control variable. For a fixed action a a , the dominant term in the backward Bellman update is the convolution with the fundamental solution Γ a ​ ( t , x , y ) \Gamma^{a}(t,x,y) . Because the elliptic operator is compact on bounded domains, the spatial update admits a rapidly decaying spectral expansion involving the eigenfunctions e k ​ ( x , a ) e_{k}(x;a) of the generator ℒ a \mathcal{L}^{a} . Critically, the true spatial eigenfunctions e k ​ ( x , a ) e_{k}(x;a) depend on a a because the diffusion tensor Σ ⁡ ( x , a ) \Sigma(x,a) and drift b ⁡ ( x , a ) b(x,a) vary with the action. Therefore, the exact global value function is not mathematically separable. However, because the dependence of the environment coefficients on a a is uniformly Lipschitz (Assumption 1 ), the manifold of spatial solutions ℳ = { Q ⁡ ( ⋅ , a ) : a ∈ 𝒜 } \mathcal{M}=\{Q(\cdot,a):a\in\mathcal{A}\} exhibits low ε \varepsilon -rank. By employing a CP decomposition, the network learns a finite, universal set of spatial basis functions { ϕ k ​ ( x ) } k = 1 p \{\phi_{k}(x)\}_{k=1}^{p} that span the dominant eigenspaces of ℒ a \mathcal{L}^{a} across all a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} . Concurrently, the action network { ψ k ​ ( a ) } k = 1 p \{\psi_{k}(a)\}_{k=1}^{p} learns the non-smooth, action-dependent mixing coefficients required to linearly combine these spatial modes. This formulation enforces a principled anisotropic inductive bias : it allocates the smooth network capacity (e.g., tanh \tanh activations) exclusively to the spatial factors ϕ k ∈ C 2 , α ​ ( 𝒮 ) \phi_{k}\in C^{2,\alpha}(\mathcal{S}) to emulate parabolic smoothing, and allocates the non-smooth capacity (e.g., ReLU activations) exclusively to the action factors ψ k ∈ C 0 , 1 ​ ( 𝒜 ) \psi_{k}\in C^{0,1}(\mathcal{A}) to capture the non-differentiable kinks of the policy landscape. This decoupling reduces the interaction complexity to 𝒪 ⁡ ( p ) \mathcal{O}(p) while efficiently parameterizing the mixed-regularity hypothesis space ℋ α , Lip \mathcal{H}^{\alpha,\text{Lip}} defined in Corollary 15 .

sections.heading: A.3 Complexity Analysis: Dimensionality and Discretization
sections.text: Standard grid-based value iteration suffers from the classic Curse of Dimensionality: to halve the approximation error, the computational cost scales as 2 d 2^{d} . Our mesh-free Neural Operator approach mitigates this scaling through the regularizing effect of diffusion, but it is subject to trade-offs regarding the time-discretization δ \delta and sensor density m m .

sections.heading: A.3.1 Reduction of Metric Entropy
sections.text: The fundamental difficulty of learning the Q-function is governed by the size of the reachable function class 𝒬 ∗ \mathcal{Q}^{*} . As established in Corollary 15 , the uniform ellipticity of the SDE ensures that 𝒬 ∗ \mathcal{Q}^{*} is a bounded subset of the anisotropic space C x 2 , α ∩ C a 0 , 1 C^{2,\alpha}_{x}\cap C^{0,1}_{a} . The Kolmogorov ϵ \epsilon -entropy (log-covering number) of the Hölder ball of radius R R in dimension d d with smoothness s s scales as log ⁡ 𝒩 ≍ ( R / ϵ ) d / s \log\mathcal{N}\asymp(R/\epsilon)^{d/s} . In our setting, the effective smoothness in the state space is s = 2 + α s=2+\alpha . Thus, the complexity scales as: Complexity ​ ( ϵ ) ∼ exp ⁡ ( C ​ ( R ϵ ) d 2 + α ) . \text{Complexity}(\epsilon)\sim\exp\left(C\left(\frac{R}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{d}{2+\alpha}}\right). (35) Compared to standard Lipschitz continuity assumptions ( s = 1 s=1 , exponent d d ), the diffusion term reduces the effective dimensionality exponent by a factor of roughly 3 3 (since 2 + α ≈ 3 2+\alpha\approx 3 ). While the dependence on d d remains exponential in the worst case (covering the entire uniform norm), the volume of the function space is significantly compressed.

sections.heading: A.3.2 Sensor Aliasing and Statistical Rates
sections.text: The DeepONet replaces the spatial grid with a set of m m scattered sensors { z j } j = 1 m \{z_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m} . The total error decomposes into the operator approximation error and the input encoding (aliasing) error: ‖ 𝒩 − 𝒯 ‖ ≤ ‖ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒫 m ​ Q ) − 𝒯 ⁡ ( ℛ ​ 𝒫 m ​ Q ) ‖ ⏟ Neural approx. error + ‖ 𝒯 ⁡ ( ℛ ​ 𝒫 m ​ Q − Q ) ‖ ⏟ Sensor encoding error , \|\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{T}\|\leq\underbrace{\|\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{P}_{m}Q)-\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{R}\mathcal{P}_{m}Q)\|}_{\text{Neural approx. error}}+\underbrace{\|\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{R}\mathcal{P}_{m}Q-Q)\|}_{\text{Sensor encoding error}}, (36) where 𝒫 m \mathcal{P}_{m} is the evaluation map and ℛ \mathcal{R} is an optimal reconstruction operator. • Worst-Case Error: To guarantee uniformly bounded error over the compact set, the sensor fill-distance h h must satisfy L ​ h α < ϵ Lh^{\alpha}<\epsilon . This requires m ∼ ϵ − d / α m\sim\epsilon^{-d/\alpha} sensors, which still suffers from the curse of dimensionality. • Generalization Error: However, in Deep RL, we minimize the L μ 2 L^{2}_{\mu} error over an exploration distribution μ \mu . By standard statistical learning theory (e.g., Rademacher complexity bounds), the generalization error scales as 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / N s ​ a ​ m ​ p ​ l ​ e ​ s ) \mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N_{samples}}) , independent of the dimension d d . The Neural Operator efficiently learns the map on the support of μ \mu , effectively breaking the curse for the visited states.

sections.heading: A.3.3 The Complexity-Stability Trade-off ( δ → 0 \delta\to 0 )
sections.text: From the Schauder estimate ( 20 ), the radius of the function class scales as R δ ∼ δ − 1 + α 2 R_{\delta}\sim\delta^{-\frac{1+\alpha}{2}} . Substituting this into the entropy bound, the required network capacity W W behaves as: W ⁡ ( δ , ϵ ) ∼ ( 1 δ 1 + α 2 ​ ϵ ) d 2 + α . W(\delta,\epsilon)\sim\left(\frac{1}{\delta^{\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{d}{2+\alpha}}. (37) This reveals a fundamental Stability-Complexity Trade-off : • Smoothing Regime (Fixed δ \delta ): For a discrete MDP with fixed step δ \delta , the operator is strongly smoothing, and the Q-functions lie on a low-complexity manifold. The network size remains manageable. • Stiff Regime ( δ → 0 \delta\to 0 ): As we approximate the continuous-time limit, the operator approaches the Identity, and the smoothing vanishes. The target functions become stiff (large second derivatives), and the required network capacity explodes. This suggests that value-based discretizations built from Bellman iteration are best conditioned when δ \delta is chosen large enough to allow diffusion to act, rather than trying to approximate the SDE with infinitesimal steps directly.

sections.heading: A.4 Recursive Residual Formulation
sections.text: For problems with long horizons (large N = T / δ N=T/\delta ), we construct the solution by recursively applying the operator. Direct composition of neural operators can lead to optimization difficulties akin to the vanishing gradient problem. However, the parabolic nature of the Bellman equation suggests a natural residual structure. Since the value function evolves continuously in time, for small δ \delta , the linear diffusion part of 𝒯 δ \mathcal{T}_{\delta} is close to the Identity; the nonlinear maximization term also requires the current action to be near-greedy for the normalized residual to remain O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) . We propose a Residual Operator architecture that learns the temporal difference rather than the absolute value.

sections.heading: A.4.1 Discrete Euler Scheme in Function Space
sections.text: Let Q ^ ( k ) \hat{Q}^{(k)} denote the approximate Q-function at time-step k k (corresponding to physical time t k = T − k ​ δ t_{k}=T-k\delta ). We formulate the update as: Q ^ ( k + 1 ) ​ ( x , a ) = Q ^ ( k ) ​ ( x , a ) + δ ⋅ 𝒩 res ​ ( Q ^ ( k ) ) ​ ( x , a ) , \hat{Q}^{(k+1)}(x,a)=\hat{Q}^{(k)}(x,a)+\delta\cdot\mathcal{N}_{\text{res}}\left(\hat{Q}^{(k)}\right)(x,a), (38) with the initialization Q ^ ( 0 ) ​ ( x , a ) = g ⁡ ( x ) \hat{Q}^{(0)}(x,a)=g(x) . Here, 𝒩 res \mathcal{N}_{\text{res}} is a DeepONet trained to approximate the normalized displacement operator: ℛ δ ​ ( Q ) ≔ 𝒯 δ ​ Q − Q δ . \mathcal{R}_{\delta}(Q)\coloneqq\frac{\mathcal{T}_{\delta}Q-Q}{\delta}. (39) From the PDE characterization in Eq. ( 15 ), the normalized residual decomposes into a local generator contribution plus a maximization-gap contribution: ℛ δ ​ ( Q ) ​ ( x , a ) = ℒ t a ​ Q ​ ( x , a ) + r ⁡ ( t , x , a ) + 1 δ ​ ( V Q ​ ( x ) − Q ⁡ ( x , a ) ) + o ⁡ ( 1 ) , \mathcal{R}_{\delta}(Q)(x,a)=\mathcal{L}^{a}_{t}Q(x,a)+r(t,x,a)+\frac{1}{\delta}\left(V_{Q}(x)-Q(x,a)\right)+o(1), (40) where V Q ​ ( x ) ≔ sup a ′ ∈ 𝒜 Q ⁡ ( x , a ′ ) V_{Q}(x)\coloneqq\sup_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q(x,a^{\prime}) , with the expansion interpreted locally for time-dependent coefficients through the parabolic evolution family. Thus the residual converges to the Hamiltonian only on the zero-gap or near-greedy regime where V Q ​ ( x ) − Q ⁡ ( x , a ) = o ⁡ ( δ ) V_{Q}(x)-Q(x,a)=o(\delta) . The residual operator network should therefore be read as learning the Hamiltonian on this active/near-active set, not as removing the Bellman maximization gap for arbitrary off-policy actions.

sections.heading: A.4.2 Advantages of the Residual Approach
sections.text: (i) Well-Conditioned Learning: In the stiff regime where δ \delta is small, the diffusion-evolution part of Q ↦ 𝒯 δ ​ Q Q\mapsto\mathcal{T}_{\delta}Q is dominated by the Identity. Learning the full map directly forces the network to expend capacity approximating this nearly identity component. The residual formulation subtracts it and focuses capacity on the dynamics, provided the maximization gap is separately controlled on the active or near-greedy action set. (ii) Flow Consistency: This architecture effectively implements a Forward Euler discretization of the abstract Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) in the Banach space ℋ α , Lip \mathcal{H}^{\alpha,\text{Lip}} : d d ​ τ ​ 𝐐 ​ ( τ ) = 𝐅 ⁡ ( 𝐐 ⁡ ( τ ) ) , 𝐐 ⁡ ( 0 ) = g , \frac{d}{d\tau}\mathbf{Q}(\tau)=\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{Q}(\tau)),\quad\mathbf{Q}(0)=g, (41) where τ \tau is time-to-go and 𝐅 \mathbf{F} is the non-linear Bellman generator. This ensures that the inductive bias of the network aligns with the physical flow of information. (iii) Iterative Stability: By sharing the weights of 𝒩 res \mathcal{N}_{\text{res}} across time-steps (Recurrent Operator Learning), we enforce that the laws of physics (the environment dynamics) remain constant, while the value function evolves. This dramatically reduces the number of parameters compared to training separate networks for each time step.

sections.heading: D.4 Realizability of the Branch Net
sections.text: Our analysis assumes the Branch Net β \beta can approximate the anisotropic Moving Least Squares (MLS) operator (Assumption 24 ). The MLS shape functions are rational functions of the input coordinates (ratios of polynomials involving the kernel weights). Recent results in approximation theory ( Telgarsky, 2017 ; Yarotsky, 2017 ) establish that deep ReLU networks can approximate rational functions with exponential convergence w.r.t. depth. Specifically, to approximate a rational function with error ε \varepsilon , a depth of 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) ) \mathcal{O}(\log(1/\varepsilon)) suffices. Thus, the assumption that standard MLPs can serve as the Branch Net encoder for the proposed architecture is well-founded, provided the network is sufficiently deep to resolve the algebraic structure of the reconstruction operator.

sections.heading: D.5 Limitations: The Persistence of the Action Curse
sections.text: Finally, we must clarify the scope of the Curse of Dimensionality mitigation. Theorem 16 demonstrates that the parabolic smoothing reduces the effective dimension of the state space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} from d d to roughly d / 3 d/3 . However, the Bellman operator provides no smoothing in the action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . The derived complexity bound: W ∼ 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ − γ ​ d ​ ε − d 2 + α + ( δ ​ ε ) − d a ) , W\sim\mathcal{O}\left(\delta^{-\gamma d}\varepsilon^{-\frac{d}{2+\alpha}}+(\delta\varepsilon)^{-d_{a}}\right), (93) retains an exponential dependence on the action dimension d a d_{a} . For high-dimensional control problems ( d a ≫ 1 d_{a}\gg 1 ), the second term dominates. Our anisotropic DeepONet architecture prevents the state dimension from contaminating the action complexity, but it cannot remove the intrinsic hardness of optimizing non-concave functions over high-dimensional action spaces. This remains a fundamental limitation of value-based methods in continuous control, suggesting that for large d a d_{a} , policy-gradient methods (which avoid explicit maximization over 𝒜 \mathcal{A} ) may be structurally necessary.

At the same time, we do not claim a full convergence theorem for practical sampled Q-learning with exploration, replay, and stochastic gradient updates. 1 1 footnotetext: Accepted for presentation at the Conference on Learning Theory (COLT) 2026. keywords Q-Learning Theory, Bellman Value Iteration, Neural Operators, Parabolic Smoothing, Stochastic Optimal Control, Approximation Theory. 1 Introduction This paper studies the operator-theoretic core of Q-learning in continuous-time stochastic control with continuous states and actions. In value-based reinforcement learning, the central object is the Bellman optimality update for the action-value function; every Q-learning or DQN step is, at heart, an attempt to approximate this update from data. Our focus is on this Bellman target itself in a continuous-time diffusion model, where the coefficients are known and the operator can be analyzed directly. This does not yet cover all ingredients of practical Q-learning, but it does address what we view as one of its core theoretical questions: what regularity and approximation complexity does the Bellman target class possess? The relationship with Q-learning can be stated concretely. In discrete time, a typical value-based target has the form r + β ​ max a ′ ⁡ Q ⁡ ( x ′ , a ′ ) r+ eta\max_{a^{\prime}}Q(x^{\prime},a^{\prime}) , namely a stochastic approximation to a Bellman optimality operator. Our continuous-time discretization replaces the single sampled transition by its conditional expectation over a short diffusion step of size δ \delta , thereby isolating the operator-level part of the theory from the separate issues of exploration, replay, and stochastic optimization. This is why we view the paper as a contribution to Q-learning theory, while also being explicit that it operates at the Bellman-operator level. Classical analyses of value-based methods with function approximation often assume that the transition and reward coefficients are globally Lipschitz in state and action. While convenient, this hypothesis misses a central feature of stochastic control: non-degenerate diffusion can regularize the Bellman update through parabolic smoothing. In PDE language, the Bellman step is tied to a controlled parabolic equation, so rough inputs may become more regular after one application of the operator ( Krylov, 1987 ) . Motivated by this observation, we study the time-discretized Bellman optimality operator 𝒯 δ \mathcal{T}_{\delta} under uniform ellipticity and Hölder-regular coefficients. The main message is that the Bellman targets underlying value-based learning in this regime lie in an anisotropic regularity class substantially smaller than a generic Lipschitz class. This creates an approximation-theoretic route toward neural architectures tailored to the regularity of continuous-control Bellman iterates, and hence toward a sharper theory of what Q-learning-style methods are trying to approximate in this setting. 1.1 Main Contributions Our contributions are fourfold. First, we prove that under uniform ellipticity the Bellman operator maps bounded inputs into an anisotropic Hölder class: smooth in the state variable and only Lipschitz in the action variable. This identifies a nontrivial regularity structure for the Bellman targets that arise in continuous-time Q-learning problems. Second, we show that this regularity statement is already a core theoretical contribution to Q-learning: it describes the target class that any value-function approximator must represent in this diffusion regime. The operator-theoretic viewpoint is therefore not peripheral to Q-learning, but rather isolates its mathematical backbone. Third, we use this regularity to derive approximation guarantees for a tensor-product DeepONet architecture that approximates Bellman iterates. The architecture is chosen because it matches the anisotropic regularity revealed by the Bellman analysis; the regularity statement itself is architecture-independent, while the theorem provides one constructive approximation route. Fourth, we quantify the stiffness–complexity trade-off induced by the time step δ \delta . As δ → 0 \delta	o 0 , the Bellman operator approaches the identity and the smoothing effect weakens, which increases the approximation complexity. This explains why continuous-time limits can become numerically stiff even when the diffusion is regularizing. Overall, the paper aims to make a precise claim: in continuous stochastic control with uniformly elliptic diffusion, the Bellman targets at the heart of Q-learning enjoy exploitable anisotropic regularity, and this has concrete consequences for approximation theory and architecture design. What we do not claim is a full convergence theorem for sampled Q-learning with exploration, replay, target-network heuristics, and stochastic gradient optimization. 1.2 Literature Review Our work sits at the intersection of approximation theory for Deep Learning, stochastic analysis of PDEs, and reinforcement learning.
